utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language that is -- that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I can. I can follow everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution team, together with Ms. Patricia Sellers and Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour and my learned friends, my name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant Ms. Jasmina Cosic and our CaseMap manager Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Madam Vidovic. Good morning to you and the rest of your team. Any preliminaries before we start? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: There is one housekeeping matter I would like to address. We received a list of the Defence exhibits yesterday evening, and the only clarification we're seeking with respect to this list is there is -- there is on the list the transcript of the Deronjic interview, and there's an indication that the Defence will be using pages 9, 10 and 11. The Prosecution would ask for further clarification because there were at least three interviews of this individual and as such a number of tapes as a result and we are seeking to establish exactly which interview, what day, and what pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that information can be easily provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the transcript of an interview held on the 23rd of June, 2003, and it's on tape 2073A, pages 9, 10, and 11 on the English transcript, as we have both the Bosnian and English versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any further remarks?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The other thing we wanted to raise ourselves is in relation to the Defence motion for -- regarding possible adjudicated facts to be taken into account. I don't know if the Prosecution is in a position to anticipate its response in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will give the floor to Ms. Patricia Sellers for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution will respond to the Defence motion. I think that we can safely inform both counsel and the Bench that we will be opposing the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Incidentally, just for the record because I also so discovered this morning that this fact was not known to my two colleagues, I was -- I composed part of the Trial Chamber that decided the Deronjic case, so that I want to put it on record that I was one of the three Judges in the Deronjic case. If there is nothing else we can bring in the witness. And also incidentally because -- I'm not saying it is related, but we're talking of more or less the same area, the same time frame. I was also one of the three Judges which handed down the sentence in the Dragan Nikolic case, so that you should know if -- I suppose you both knew this, but I'm just putting it down for the record. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have only a minor issue, a minor request. It is from last week. We kept in the neighbourhood of this courtroom the originals of our exhibits handed -- we handled last week, meaning that they are available on short notice, but that's a kind of everyday organising. Is it possible to -- with the allowance of the parties to put them, those originals back again in the lockers of the AV unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't ask us, you know. We're not going to tell you yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Through you, Your Honour, I'll ask Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only thing, Mr. Wubben, is this, that I suppose the best thing would be to keep them under lock and key where they belong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the rule that should be followed. And then if the Defence intend calling or requesting for production of the original, I would suggest that you inform the Prosecution beforehand, at least a day before, saying, "We will be contesting the -- or for our purposes we require the original," and you will have a good time, realtime within which to bring these documents either up or down because I don't know where they are kept. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's a fine arrangement. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the rule should be that once you've finished with them here they should go back to where they belong and not kept in any other place. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because in that case you would be responsible for their custody if you retained them under your custody, and I don't think you should shoulder that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you are receiving interpretation of what I am saying in a language that you can understand. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So welcome to this Tribunal, and I thank you for having come over to give testimony. Before you start giving evidence, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration, something similar and certainly equivalent to a oath. The purpose of this declaration is to get you to state formally that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper that the lady who is standing next to you, Madam Usher, will be handing to you. Please read out that declaration aloud and that will be your solemn declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I will try to explain very briefly what's going to happen. You will be first asked a series of questions by Madam Richardson from the side of the Prosecution, who have called you as a witness, and when that set of questions is finished, I hope at the end of the -- by the end of this first session before the break, after that you will be cross-examined by Madam Vidovic who is appearing for the defendant in this case, Naser Oric. At the end there maybe some questions from us here. I wish to remind you of something which is fundamental. The moment you have taken your place there and sat down on that chair, you are no longer a witness of the Prosecution. You are a witness of this Tribunal, carrying the responsibility and also the duty to speak the truth. And in giving us your version of the events in answering the questions that are put to you, your duty is to answer fully and truthfully every question that is put to you irrespective of who is putting the question to you, irrespective of whether it's coming from the Prosecution or from the Defence. The important thing is that you answer fully and truthfully. So I now invite Ms. Richardson to put her question to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milo Rankovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what is your marital status?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's good.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have three.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how old are they?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: One was born in 1977, the other one in 1978, and the third one in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Where in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in what municipality is Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you live in any particular hamlet in Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The new part of Jezestica called Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How long have you resided in Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Since 1953. I was born there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a joiner, but I am also a salesman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, could you describe the village of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Describe the village of Jezestica in relation to which period of time, now or --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In 1992, how many village -- how many houses are contained in the village of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the old part 54, and in the new part about 60 or so. These were new buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many people resided in Jezestica in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in the beginning of that year, we all lived in Jezestica, some of us in the old part and some of us in the new part. And there were 512 inhabitants according to the list of inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And that included residents in the old and in the new part of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. All of that was called Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what is the ethnic make-up of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Purely Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And your ethnicity is also Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would ask the usher to hand an exhibit. I should first ask -- I should first say that what I'm holding in my hand is a map. I'd ask that it be pre-marked for identification and assigned a number for the Prosecution. I understand that the Defence already has copies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Ms. Richardson, I'm suggesting to my colleagues to close a blind eye for today, but I don't want to see this kind of thing. This is giving -- this is giving evidence, giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The moment you say Jezestica, okay, where Jezestica is, it's harmless, but the moment you say attacked 8th of August, 1992, you're making a statement that you shouldn't make in one of the documents you're tendering in evidence. I am allowing it because basically I don't think the issue will arise whether there was an attack on the 8th of August or not. The question is who attacked who and whether -- what kind of an attack it was. But if there is an objection on the part of the Defence, I will ask you to withdraw this and replace it by a proper map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do object to this document for another reason also. We ask that in future such large markings be not included in the map, because apart from suggesting what happened, the lettering covers an important part of the map, one that's important for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So how easy is it for you to replace it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not a problem. We can replace it as soon as we have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In the meantime, can we make use of it, Madam Vidovic, for the purpose of this witness and then have it replaced later?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for being practical in your approach. I think I sent a message. This is the second time this has happened. The first time was with photos with an indication of what the photo represented underneath. There will not be a third time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, what you see in front of you marked for identification as Prosecution Exhibit 377, and I would ask you to take a look at it and ask if you've seen it before. Have you seen this map before?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, if you take --

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm seeing it now for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. If you take a look at it for a moment, is there -- can you seem the village of Jezestica on that map?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as you look at the surrounding area of Jezestica as indicated on the map, can you see the hamlets contained in Jezestica in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Jezestica is noted here, but I don't see the hamlets. The centre is down there, and then you can see Kjevici, Djermani, and Rankovici and all the other hamlets if you climb up the hill, and it's about half an hour's walk. However, if you're in Polje, the new part, then you don't see those hamlets from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how far away is the new part of town from the old part of town, distance?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The new part from the centre, from my house where I was, of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. new part of the village of Jezestica, it's half an hour's walk to all these hamlets, all these Djermani, Kijevici, Rankovici, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I just bring your attention back to this map, there are some hamlets reflected on this map but not all?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Djermani is here, but not all of them, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the surrounding areas, and by that I mean the areas that are surrounding Jezestica, the other villages?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Siljkovici, then there's Kravica or Opravdici, Mandici, Colakovici. All these villages are around Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what is the ethnic make-up of those villages? And we can start with Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can start.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What is the ethnic make-up? Are they --

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic make-up of Siljkovici is Serbian, Kravica, of course, Popovici, Colokovici, Orcenovici, Opravdici, all of those are Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how far away is the nearest Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The nearest Muslim village is Sandici in the direction of Konjevic Polje, and then there's Glogova in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I have another map. I would ask that a number be assigned for identification, and we have copies for -- the Defence already has copies of the maps, but there are additional copies present. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P394.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, what you're holding in front of you --

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just take another pair of glasses, please. Yes, we can go now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Have you seen what is now marked for identification as Prosecution's Exhibit 394 before? Have you ever seen this map?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you look at the map for a moment, can you tell me if Jezestica is represented on that map?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And can you also see some of the surrounding villages and municipalities on that map?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I would -- if I may, we can have the -- the map placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, could you look at this map and tell us what is the ethnic make-up for the village of Kravica on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Serbian village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The village of Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Muslim village, but there are three Serbian houses at the very edge of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a mixed community.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a minority of Serbs. The majority was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that -- that there is a Muslim village as close to the village of Jezestica. And correct me if I'm wrong if it's a village or a hamlet. Could you point exactly to -- on the map where that village or hamlet is located, if you can?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Close to Jezestica village?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's Mocila [phoen] near Magasici. It was a hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you assist us by pointing to where it, in your estimation, it would be located on this map?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Between Jezestica in the direction of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I -- Madam Usher is -- if she can assist you in pointing to exactly where on the map and if you can point to it.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you just put an X or some indication as to where this village is located.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And could he put now his initials next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you put the initial of your first name and your last name next to that mark.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now just returning to the village of Jezestica for a moment. What type of public facilities do you have -- or did you have - excuse me - in Jezestica in 1992? And by that I mean were there any schools, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, we just had a reading room financed by the villagers, and we put a memorial plaque with the names of the people killed in the war, and that was on the wall of the reading room. We also held meetings there, had vaccination campaigns for children and other conventions, and we also sat there and watched television.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have a police station or school or any other public facility?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. The nearest police station was in Bratunac and an elementary school in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have relatives residing in the village other than your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: All of us lived there. We went to work from there. Some worked in Kravica, some worked in Bratunac, and a lot of us worked in the field as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have any relatives? You mentioned your wife and children. Did you have any other relatives residing in Jezestica? In 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had relatives. Younger people worked in the field, elderly people lived in the village, and we all shared common surnames.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have any immediate members of your family, a mother or an immediate family living in the village other than relatives, other than maybe distant relatives, but did your mother or father also reside in Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: I lived with my mother and my father's sister. They lived in the old part of Jezestica, and I built a new house in Polje where my wife and our three children lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there were at least one Muslim village close to Jezestica. Could you tell us what type of relationship the members of your village had with the members of the Muslim villages in the surrounding area? In other words --

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The hamlet of Mocila, which is part of the Serbian Magasici village, we went on very well before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what happened when the war broke out? Did this change the relationship?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course the relationship changed. Not exactly the sentiments among the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, do you remember any particular event in early 1992 that changed the relationship between the -- the members -- the residents in your village and the surrounding Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, early 1992, in mid-April, we felt that our neighbours, for example a forest keeper who passed through our village, there was a feeling of uneasiness. I don't know what was the root of that. I couldn't say. The emotions were something -- were different from April onwards. They were not the same as they had been in 1990 or 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did the members of your village take any action as a result of this change in the relationship with your neighbouring -- with the neighbouring Muslim villagers?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I cannot say that we have undertaken anything. It wasn't a normal situation. There was no cooperation, as they had to -- they used to come to plough our fields. And of course certain changes did occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your village established a village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Village guards were established in mid-April, and due to that feeling of uneasiness, we heard different things. It was not properly organised but just -- we just -- we were just kind of vigilant in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, why don't you explain to us exactly the -- the make-up of the village guard. Who was in the village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: For example, every hamlet, and I am from the hamlet Rankovici, there were ten or 12 of us, and we were on duty or just kept patrolling above the village due to the fear that we felt.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who organised the village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: We organised ourselves. I cannot pinpoint anyone in particular. We just sat together, ten or 12 of us from that hamlet, and we agreed to patrol the area during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And why did you establish this village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The reason was fear, because we heard that they were keeping their guards. So that was simply the -- the simple reason was fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you say "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us whether the village guard had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a problem with the interpretation. We did not get a single word of what the witness said in reply to the question that was put to him. And I don't know if I am being heard by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. These things happen. Sir, we had a problem with the interpretation. We did not have translation of your reply to the question put to you by Madam Richardson. I am going to read out again the question that was put to you and then could you please answer it again. The question was: "Now, could you tell us whether the village guard had any weapons?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We had our own weapons, licensed shotguns, pistols, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where did you get these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Those were licensed weapons. We were members of the hunting club, and we held those weapons in our homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you had these weapons prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, before 1992. Some people had weapons for 20 years. I cannot say exactly for every particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you have uniforms that you would wear while on patrol?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We -- and I am speaking for myself, I served military service in 1972 and came back in 1973. I was issued an army uniform in 1974 because we had normal drills thereafter in Han Pijesak and other places. A dozen of us from my village went to these exercises and drills in 1976, for example, and I kept -- we kept these uniforms at home. So whenever we received summons every second year we put on those uniforms but we kept them in our houses. We didn't have any other uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a few minutes ago that there were 12 people in the village guard, 12 men. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you explain to us how yourself and these other individuals patrolled the village?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: We just walked above the village from one end to the other end. We just passed through the village, and that was about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when did this take place, what time of day or night?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: During the day, we worked normally. The passage was free. But only with the first darkness we went out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how did one go about joining the village guard? Was this a volunteer type service or was it required?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No one required that, because we in our village or hamlet of Rankovici, we just sat together, the ten or 12 of us, and we agreed to whether we are going to keep watch or not. There was no single organiser among us. We just had a brotherly agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you recall the approximate ages of the men who were part of the village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, there were elderly men who had served in the military. We didn't want to have young boys. Maybe two or three men were over 60 or 70 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you established the village guard - when I say "you," not necessarily you, but when the village guard was established - did you receive any assistance from the VRS, the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you receive any uniforms from them?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Services?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Who would have given us money?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, were you ever mobilised by the Serb army, VRS? During 1992 to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Not in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In 1992 were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps he can tell us because, from the tone of his answer, he was indeed mobilised at some point in time. It seems to have been certainly not in 1992 and not in 1993. So perhaps he can tell us when he was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, can you tell us when -- if you were not mobilised in 1992 or 1993, when, if at all, you were indeed mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The whole time I spent in the village of Jezestica, in my village. In the Rankovici hamlet, as is my last name, incidentally, and I spent the whole time there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. Were you ever contacted by the Serb army at any point after the conflict began and advised that you had to serve the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you receive any documentation that indicated that you were part of the Serb army or mobilised by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. I bring your attention to August of 1992. Do you recall what occurred in your village?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, 1992, I was at home in Polje. We were working as normally, and then I heard a detonation from the direction of Djermani and Kijevici, the Serb hamlets. I went up with my cousin Mile. We climbed up a hill, and two or three hours later the women, children, men, everyone came down to the area called Polje. The people who had been up there said they had been attacked, that everything was burning. I didn't see that because I wasn't there. And then two or three hours later, we went to see what was happening from the direction of Brdo. Five or six of us went to one side, and when we climbed up a hill near the cemetery where my village of Rankovici is, we saw that everything had been burnt. There was still smoke and flames rising from the houses. Everything had been burnt down, the old part. From the top of that hill you could see Kijevici and Djermani and all these other hamlets just as you could see the hill called Gajice on the right-hand side. You could see Rankovici, Djermani, and Kijevici on the other side, and we counted 45 houses. They had all been burnt except Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for one house which was a new house and it was empty and that one stayed intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall what time of the day the attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Between 11.00 and 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And again, could you tell us what led you to believe that there was attack taking place?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: We thought there was an attack because you could hear the detonation. And after that shooting started right after the detonation. We all had weapons. Who was shooting, well, you needed half an hour to get down, and the people who fled from the burning houses came down and they told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what -- what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: They said they had been attacked from such-and-such an area. Djermani had been attacked from the direction of the village of Jaglici. Rankovici had been attacked from the side of Dijecila [phoen], Cizmici and so on. So they were attacked from that side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did they give or tell you who attacked them?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell us who had attacked them. They just said they had been attacked from the direction of the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did they tell you whether it was an army or civilians attacking them?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't say it was an army. I even heard people say that they were all in civilian -- it was all mixed, a mixed uniform. It was a mixture of civilian clothes, camouflage uniforms, olive-grey uniforms. And that happened on both sides that there was this kind of mixture of clothing. So nobody said it was an army attacking.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But did they indicate that there were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't say it was soldiers, because everybody put on what they had, parts of uniforms and other clothes. So they didn't say it was a single uniform, that the uniforms were all the same. Everybody was wearing whatever they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did they give any indication as to the ethnicity of the people that were attacking them?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't say that, but these people burst out of the woods in the direction of those villages, coming from the direction of those villages. They frightened the people, and of course the women and children fled. And in my hamlet, as well as in Djermani and Kijevici, well, my people saw them taking away food and cattle and other livestock from those houses. That was in my village of Rankovici. After that, in Djermani and Jecmista they killed two brothers and their mother, Dragan Mladjenovic and Andjelko Mladjenovic and their mother Savka Mladjenovic. They killed them. And in Rankovici they killed my brother and my uncle who was on his way from Maljine, and he was killed in a garden. Those were the two casualties we had in Rankovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. If I can just bring your attention back to what you just mentioned pertaining to where the attacks came from. You mentioned that they -- you were told that the individuals came from certain villages, the people who attacked Jezestica. What were those villages? Did they mention that to you? What direction?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Cizmici they attacked Rankovici and from the direction of Jaglici and Susnjari they attacked Djermani and Kijevici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what is the ethnic make-up of those villages?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you - if I could have Madam Usher's assistance - could you point to where on the map? And this is Prosecution Exhibit 394 where you were told that the attackers attacked from, what direction, if you can identify it?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: From here that's where Jaglici is, and from this part that's where Cizmici is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And those are Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the -- for the record, the witness indicates an area at -- between Glogova and Jezestica on the right-hand side of these two villages on the map on which he previously put his initials. That is P394.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back just a bit. You testified that you were able to see the attack taking place in the old part of the village. Could you tell us exactly where you were when you were able to observe the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: When the attack started, I said I was at home. After the burnings, we -- two or three hours after that, I climbed up to the cemetery near my village of Rankovici. And from the top of that hill you could see Kijevici, Djermani, and Rankovici burning. The people who had fled to us told us about the attack. I didn't see the attack itself, but only afterwards when I went to get my brother and my uncle, three or four hours after the attack, after they had finished burning and looting, we went up there and collected their bodies and brought their bodies down to Polje. I am speaking of the hamlet of Rankovici now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was the -- you said you went back to the village -- you went to the village about half an hour after the attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think he said three or four hours after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you observe when you went to the village, the old part, yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: First we climbed up to the top of the hill from which you could see all those hamlets, and then we looked around and patrolled around a little to see what was happening, and they had withdrawn in the direction of Cizmici back in the direction from which they had attacked, and then we collected the bodies of my brother and my uncle and carried them back to Polje, to our houses, which had not been burnt at that time. And while we organised the carrying of these bodies and the collection of the corpses, after we had done this, in the evening the village guards returned up there because we were afraid there might be another attack and that the new part of the village might be attacked. We were in the grip of fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you able to observe the condition of the houses in the old part of the town while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. These were old-fashioned houses. They were old. They were made of wood, and every house had been burnt down to the ground, to the basement. When I was interviewed in Milici for the first time, I don't remember the name of the gentleman who interviewed me in 2001, but he went with me to walk along this line. He asked me if I would accompany him, and I did. I took him to the line we held, and I showed him the entire line. I showed him the view of Jecmista, Djermani, and Kijevici and where the late Andjelko's head had been cut off, and I had showed them where that had been. And I don't know if he's here still, but he can confirm what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you also mention that you were told that livestock had been carried away. Could you tell us a little bit more about exactly what was told to you about what was taken from the old town during that attack?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we climbed up to the cemetery, the people who were there holding guard at that line, when the burning started and the shooting, they were afraid, but they observed what was happening. And they heard shouting, yelling, things being taken out of houses. And then there were ox and cows, calves, sheep, everything that a farmer normally has, all this was being taken away. And they saw -- people from my village saw them driving off the cattle and livestock in the direction of Cizmici. So we thought it was people from those villages. I don't know about Djermani. The people there would know. But I'm sure that their livestock were being taken off in the direction of Jaglici. I didn't see them going in the direction of Glogova or some other villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Richardson, just to draw your attention, since I made it clear we will have to finish with this witness today, how much more do you reckon you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think at least another 45 minutes, possibly less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break at 10.30, and then I can only give you 15 minutes more after that, because that would be exactly dividing the time equally between the two parties and leaving enough time for us to ask questions if we need to. So you have 25 -- just less than 25 plus 15. Try to finish in those.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, let's just come to where you testified that there were bodies recovered from this first attack. Do you remember the names of the individuals who died in the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: I will never forget them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll start with my hamlet of Rankovici. Srecko Rankovic and Milan Rankovic. From Djermani and Kijevici, Dragan Mladjenovic, Andjelko Mladjenovic, whose head was severed, Slavka Mladjenovic, Slavka Stjepanovic, Milosav Stjepanovic, Vojin Bogicevic, Serbo Djuric. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, what condition were the bodies in?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies -- well, for example, my brother had been pierced by a bullet, as had my uncle. When we got up to where this had happened, I went back to Kijevici and we found the late Dragan, and his head had been cut off. We found the case of his pistol for which he had a licence. We didn't find his mother Savka until about ten days later when we were searching the garden, and then we found some hair and some clothes among the weeds in the garden. That's what we found of her. My brother's legs had been broken. Dragan Mladjenovic was his name. The others were all shot with bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, where were these bodies recovered? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies were found -- my brother's body was found exactly 30 metres above our house. And most probably while we were doing that they shot at us. They were -- got afraid, and they left the body there. And he was closest to the firing place, and we had hard time going closer and recovering his body. Whereas for the other bodies, we brought them to -- all of them to Polje, the new part of Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you mention that you had found the body of Andjelko Mladjenovic and his head had been -- I'm sorry, why don't you tell us what condition his body was in?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already said that his head was severed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's also, Your Honour, that I know on the last occasion this subject came up that Your Honours were prepared to hear evidence of people having died, but is it really necessary to enter into possibly gory details?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why she is asking the question, because she has already mentioned that this gentleman Andjelko Mladjenovic had been decapitated. There are further details that you want to know I'm not going to stop you, but are they relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead then. Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you discover what happened -- did you ever recover the head of Mr. Mladjenovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rather was it -- does he know whether it had, because why does it -- did it have to be him to recover it. Ask him whether it had did it have to be him to recover it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Or anyone. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know if the head of Andjelko Mladjenovic was ever recovered?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. His head was never found. I dressed his body. I have seen how he had been beheaded, and the injuries on his brother, and we in fact never recovered them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you at any -- did you at any point come to learn what happened to this head?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, we didn't know. There were rumours that it had been taken to Srebrenica. There was an article in Novosti describing that it had been carried through Srebrenica, but I myself didn't see that. It was just a newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may at this time, I would like to have a document marked for identification, and I would have copies available for -- I believe Defence counsel has -- was already provided with copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose this is the document that you referred to - one of you - yesterday --.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- as being an additional document, no? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We wondered if there was a date or some further details about of that article because we see none on the face of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we're having the witness testify from what was presented to us yesterday by him. We're in the process of determining exactly when this article was published. But for the time being, we're simply going to present what was given to us by the witness. And also I would like to have it tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may ask one question. The Prosecution is probably delivering some different articles. What we had received from them yesterday is an incomplete article. It doesn't say which publication or which date it bears. So if everyone else has this kind of document, then I object to it being like that. We don't know the source. We don't know the date when it was published.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand Defence counsel's objection. As I said before, we're tendering this document as it was given to us by this witness. It pertains to his account of the events and what he later learned about the -- what happened to the head of the individual that died. It certainly is probative and relevant to our case with respect to the attacks as well as the presence. We will, Your Honour, in the interests of best evidence to present to the Court, determine exactly when this article was published and we will, as we are in the process of trying to determine exactly when this was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's being admitted as it is now with the understanding that you will do your utmost to provide more information on where and when this was -- was published. Failing which, obviously, there will be the normal consequences you would expect in the circumstances. Mr. Registrar, I'm giving you this. I suggest the Prosecution will tell you exactly how they intend to present it, whether they are going to fix it to -- I don't know. It's up to them, not to me. And what number shall we give it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P395.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm tendering the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually they tender the original. Usually they tender the original. The thing is this: Whether it should then be tendered like that or whether it should be stuck or partly glued to a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's up to you. I'm not going to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will ensure that this is preserved in a way that can be used by Your Honours later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, both sides, because other side which may not be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relevant as far as contents are concerned may be relevant to establish the authenticity when you later on provide the source.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, I would ask you to take a look at the newspaper article that's in front of you. Are you familiar with this article? Are you familiar with that article, Prosecution's Exhibit 395?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: This article, yes, it is familiar to me and what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When did you receive this article?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive it. I don't know whether it was a year or two ago while I was reading the press from my neighbours, and through the conversation, they found out that I was supposed to be questioned. His relatives just asked me, "Milo, could you please take some evidence with you to corroborate these rumours that were circulating."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And what does this article pertain to?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: It pertains to, I don't know, these stories, and there are some historical data there referring to our reading house. And in the Second World War, there were 144 victims whose names were carved in the plaque, but the plaque was in the meantime broken. So the journalist who wrote this made a connection there, and that's how I came about to learn about this story.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What is the title of the article?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: "Head As A Trophy."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who's head is being referred to in the article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to proceed along those lines. We can read the article.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, provided the translation is not being contested as accurate, then we can, we can --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I would rather hear the witness say is whether he knows from which newspaper this was cut. And relatively if he can indicate to us the time when this article was published.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, do you know what newspaper published this article and when it was published?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the newspaper called Vecernje Novosti, or evening news, but as to the date, I can't say, but it's definitely Vecernje Novosti.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you -- do you think it was published more or less at the time, say, in the period 1992, 1993, or is it a recent -- more recent article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. It was published certainly after the year 2000. 2002 or 2003. I cannot say. I cannot be precise on that. I made an oath to tell the truth, and I'm not going to invent any dates that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only know that it was the Vecernje Novosti newspaper, but as for the date, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: There is -- I just have one last question regarding the article, Your Honour. There is a sort of witness -- Mr. Radenko [sic], there is a picture on this article. Could you tell us who this picture is, who's in the picture?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the picture of Andjelko. I know him. He is my wife's relative, he was, and I knew him ever since he was a child. So I watched him going to school, to Kravica. He passed by my house every day and we were very closely related.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just in the interests of time, I could move along. Thank you, Ms. Usher. Mr. Radenko, I would like to bring your attention to January of 1993. Do you recall what happened in your village during that period?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1993, on the 7th of January I was also at home. That was Christmas. My mother, my father's sister were there. We were preparing things for holiday just like everybody else. And at around 5.30, we heard one strong detonation coming from the direction of Djermani hamlet and other villages. It was something unusual. Nobody expected that. And when someone gets frightened, we burst out of our houses. We gathered together. And then after about half an hour, the people who were holding the line, they all came from the two sides, Kijevici, Djermani, Rankovici, Potkonici and other hamlets. And they also again went downwards in fear, and they were fleeing saying, "We have been attacked again." So the crowd of us withdrew to two sides towards Kravica. And of course we wanted to pull out. We passed by the river, which is also called Jezestica. We stopped there at the house of Goran Djuric. It is by the asphalt road, and that is where we stopped. There were some 50 people plus and some 15 women on that side, whereas on the side of Kijevici and Djermani, they walked along the left side, and we were on the right side. So we remained there for some time looking at the houses burning, and that was a repetition of the previous event. The whole of Jezestica was on fire, and we saw people. We heard shots. We saw people entering the house. I saw some 20 people going into my house where they spent about 20 or 30 minutes. Then they carried out things. Although it was far away, but I could see that they were taking out my fridge and whatever they needed. I couldn't see if they were collecting any cutleries. They just collected what they wanted. That was for my house. As for the people who withdrew to Djermani and Kijevici, they everybody's house on fire, and the entire village -- that section of the village of Jezestica was burnt on the 7th of January. So all of us were safe. Nobody got killed on that line. We stayed at Goran Djuric's house, and after that we tried to withdraw towards Drina. Those who were killed were killed within 200 metres of Goran Djuric's house, and that is where there were -- their dead bodies were found on the 23rd of March, where we came to undig them because they were buried either in the shallow ground or somewhat deeper. So we managed to find some of them. Some we didn't. Among them was Drago Lazic. And also my mother's father and uncle were killed in their houses. And Radomir Jovanovic is still missing. We never found his remains, and we assume that he was killed. We just found his army jacket, nothing else, and some underwear, but the body was never recovered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, could you tell us -- could you describe for us the attackers, what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The attackers, as much as we could see because there was a field covered with snow, but as much as I can tell, they were dressed in white uniforms. Some had similar to the ones we had on. And also civilian clothes and some camouflage clothes. So when they came, a couple of them had horse-driven carts, and there was a layer of snow. They were pulling out oxen carts, agriculture machinery, cookers, and things that they just wanted. While they were carrying that out, we could see whether a house was entered by a person in a white uniform or in civilian clothes. We also saw some women carrying things from the houses, bed linen and things like that. I couldn't see any particular details like a frying-pan or smaller items like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When -- when the attack occurred, were the women present? The women that you just testified were carrying things away, were they present or did they come later on?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: They came later on. The first stage they drove us out, then first men come to carry things out, then women come to take things out, and then they set houses on fire. So they drove all those items away, but I don't know where they took them. I didn't have time to -- to wait and see where they would end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the ethnicity of the women or the people who were attacking the village?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: The men and women and their ethnicity, we recognised the women by the dresses they wore, the costumes they wore, and men looked like men. For example, if they were to say otherwise and to tell that our women wore skirts and their women wore dimije, which is a kind of trousers or pantaloons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So what was the ethnicity of the women that you could identify?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims because they had these dimije on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the men that were carrying items or things out of the houses that you observed, were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: As I told you, there were three types of clothes, just like we did. Before the outbreak of the war, we were all together, and we wore the same uniforms, drab olive winter uniforms. They also had white uniforms or clothes, and some of them were in civilian clothes. So I saw three types of clothes, the white ones, the uniforms, and the civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you. Most probably there were lots of them because they managed to burn more than 60 houses. Therefore, there must have been many of them, because this area is quite large around Kravica. So viewing from Rankovici as far as to Djermani, Kijevici and downwards to Gradac and other places, it's a huge area. I saw some 20 people coming downhill from Jezestica after the attack. Some other people saw other men at different locations. I personally saw about 50 or 60 men approaching the houses across this clearing, but some people -- my co-villagers saw some other people at some other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to stop here for a break. I thank you, sir. You will be escorted by Madam Usher. We will have a 25-minute break. Thank you. We'll start at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, with respect to the attack that took place in August of 1992, August 8 specifically, and January of 1993, did you ever learn who the leader was of the individuals who attacked your village?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would object to that question. In evidence, this witness has referred to a mixture of attackers whom he didn't actually see himself dealing, first of all, with the 8th of August. He learnt from various people what had happened. For the January 1993 action, he referred to civilians, women, people in all sorts of different uniforms. There is no suggestion anywhere that this witness might have any first hand knowledge firstly that these people were organised into any sort of a group, that -- had any sort of a leader. He's being invited to speculate. That's what I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will see whether he will be speculating or not depending on what knowledge he has, so let him answer the question and then depending on the question we will draw conclusions. Whether it is mere speculation, but this is the system, again, for you and for me it sounds a little bit high-handed, the way the question has been put, but the system how it works here is exactly the opposite of what we are used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand that. It's just from his evidence this morning it seems a huge leap to go to a leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, but you will need to learn to be patient like I do. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because at the end of the day, since most of the -- or a good chunk of the evidence is based on hearsay here, at the end of the day you took it home with you and you put it in the appropriate pigeonhole and then later on in the day you decide if you're going to give it any importance at all, whether you consider it hearsay evidence worth -- worth considering, worth having probative value, in other words, or whether it's just hearsay amounting to speculation and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's just to register our concern about that speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately the situation is like that. I'm not used to it, you're not used to it. But I have been here doing this three years and I have got used and I control myself. Thanks, Mr. Jones, anyway for pointing that. Yes, I suppose you will repeat the question, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I apologies for interrupting you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rankovic, did there come a time that you learned who was responsible or the leader of the individuals who attacked the village in August, and then further with respect to the attack, in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know exactly who was the leader. What do I know? I can't tell you the name of the person. I didn't see him either on the 8th of August. Well, if I had seen him, he would have killed me, of course. I heard that there was a leader of the Serbian army. I heard of a certain Naser Oric, but I neither saw him nor do I know the man. I just heard about him. I did not see any of the attackers. I can't say whether it was Huso, Haso, or Meho. I didn't see any of my neighbours from Jaglici, Susnjari or Glogova, so I can't say I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question. You testified that you heard there was a leader of the Serbian army. Is it the Serbian army or the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: You want me to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No. I'm asking -- actually I can rephrase --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reading the transcript of what you said it says here that you said, "I heard that there was a leader of the Serbian army." Did you say that or did you say, "I heard that there was a leader of the Muslim army"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was just as there was a leader of the Serb army whose name I don't know, there was also a leader of the Muslim army. I heard that this was Naser Oric, but I don't wish to speculate because I neither saw nor heard him, and I don't know him. I didn't see Huso or Haso or anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, the attackers that you observed in January, in your opinion were they acting as a group? Were they together?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: They divided into groups. One group came from the direction of Jezestica. Jezestica has four hamlets. There's Polje, there's a part called Gradac in the direction of Glogova. Then there's Rankovici in the centre. To the right there's Kijevici and Djermani. We were attacked from all sides, Siljkovici and so on, from the direction of the villages around Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richardson, you have got not more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rankovic, when you were attacked, you fled the village at some point in January of 1993, your village?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We fled in the direction of the River Drina. That was on the 7th of January, 1993. The women went to Bratunac to stay with their relatives and friends because everything had been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: While you were fleeing, did you observe anything in the direction that you were fleeing? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived at a plateau in the direction of Branjevici there was a hill called Sampon [phoen]. From there you could see the whole area. You can't see Kravica because it's in the valley, but you can see Siljkovici, all of Jezestica, Mandici, Opravdici, all that part around those villages. And we saw them burning. Everything was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what is the ethnicity of these villages that were on fire?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you returned to Jezestica following that attack in January, on January 7th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't go back to Jezestica. That evening we men stayed on that plateau and that's where we were until the 23rd. And then we went back. We didn't actually go back, but a pathologist arrived to collect the remains, and then I went by my house because we wanted to see the condition our houses were in. So I passed by my house. I saw some graffiti in my garage, and I saw that mortars had been placed there because my mother and I found some packaging behind the garage where our water fountain is. And then my mother went back to stay with her sister in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You said you -- you just testified you saw some graffiti. Could you tell us what kind of graffiti? Did it say anything?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: It said "SDA." It's still there in my garage, in my cellar. I didn't paint over or whitewash it. They were there. They probably slept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what is SDA?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: What, do I know what SDA is?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know what it stands for, SDA? Is it some kind of organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: What do I know? It's like a party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MILO RANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a Muslim designation. I can't speculate about it. I just read the letters S-D-A on my wall. It's still there. You can still see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you?
